Given an age in seconds, say how old someone would be on each planet of the Solar System.

Adapted from Exercism's [problem specification](https://github.com/exercism/problem-specifications/tree/main/exercises/space-age) (MIT). Listed under [Numbers & Math](/examples/?subject=numbers-and-math).

```nomi-run
// FILE: space_age.nomi
//# How old someone would be on each planet of the Solar System.

once earth_year_seconds = 31_557_600.0

/// A planet of the Solar System.
pub enum Planet {
    Mercury
    Venus
    Earth
    Mars
    Jupiter
    Saturn
    Uranus
    Neptune
}

impl Planet {
    /// The planet named `name`, such as `"Mars"`, or `None` for a name that
    /// is not one of the eight.
    pub fn parse(name: String) -> Maybe<Planet> {
        Planet.variants() |> Iter.find(&("${&1}" == name))
    }

    /// How long the planet takes to orbit the Sun, in Earth years.
    pub fn orbital_period(planet: Planet) -> Float {
        case planet {
            .Mercury -> 0.2408467
            .Venus -> 0.61519726
            .Earth -> 1.0
            .Mars -> 1.8808158
            .Jupiter -> 11.862615
            .Saturn -> 29.447498
            .Uranus -> 84.016846
            .Neptune -> 164.79132
        }
    }
}

derive Display for Planet
derive Variants for Planet

/// The age, in the planet's years, of someone `seconds` old.
pub fn age(planet: Planet, seconds: Int) -> Float {
    earth_years = Int.to_float(seconds) / earth_year_seconds
    earth_years / Planet.orbital_period(planet)
}

// FILE: space_age_test.nomi
import {
    space_age
    space_age.Planet
}

test "age" {
    cases = [
        #("age on Earth", Planet.Earth, 1000000000, 31.69),
        #("age on Mercury", .Mercury, 2134835688, 280.88),
        #("age on Venus", .Venus, 189839836, 9.78),
        #("age on Mars", .Mars, 2129871239, 35.88),
        #("age on Jupiter", .Jupiter, 901876382, 2.41),
        #("age on Saturn", .Saturn, 2000000000, 2.15),
        #("age on Uranus", .Uranus, 1210123456, 0.46),
        #("age on Neptune", .Neptune, 1821023456, 0.35),
    ]

    subtests cases, #(description, planet, seconds, expected), description {
        assert Float.round(space_age.age(planet, seconds), 2) == expected
    }
}

// Not canonical: the canonical data names planets only as inputs to `age`.
test "planet names" {
    assert Planet.parse("Neptune") == Some(.Neptune)
}

test "invalid planet causes error" {
    assert Planet.parse("Sun") == None
}
```

## How it's written

- The planets are a `Planet` enum, and `age` takes one, so an age on a planet that does not exist cannot be asked for. The canonical "not a planet" case becomes `Planet.parse("Sun") == None`; the test file adds one non-canonical case that `parse` finds a planet.
- `Planet.parse` finds the variant whose `derive Display` name matches, over `derive Variants`' list, instead of a `case` with eight string arms that repeat the variant names.
- `Planet.parse` returns a `Maybe`, not a `Result`: a name either names a planet or it does not, and there is only one way to fail.
- The orbital periods are a `case` in `Planet.orbital_period`, so adding a planet without its period is a missing arm.
- The canonical ages are given to two decimal places, so the tests round the computed age with `Float.round(age, 2)` and compare exactly. The rounded Float is the one nearest the two-decimal value, which is the Float the expected literal reads as.
- The table's first row names `Planet.Earth`; later rows write bare variants, which take the enum of the first row's column.
